abstract.p: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy is a rapidly expanding key therapeutic category, originally pioneered for haematological malignancies, now being developed into treatments for solid tumours and non-malignant immune-mediated conditions. Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies have some relatively unique toxicities which can affect the liver, in addition to potential drug-induced liver injury and hepatitis B virus reactivation. This manuscript was developed by the IQ Consortium (International Consortium for Innovation and Quality in Pharmaceutical Development) Drug-induced Liver Injury (DILI) Initiative that consists of members from 17 pharmaceutical companies, in collaboration with academic and regulatory DILI experts. The aim was to produce a comprehensive guide to summarise the hepatic effects of CAR-T, and to propose an approach to the investigation of liver test changes. The clinical characteristics of liver test changes in association with cytokine release syndrome and immune-effector cell haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis are described, to enable these anticipated hepatic effects to be distinguished from other causes of abnormal liver tests. The frequency and timing of many primary and secondary liver conditions that may present after CAR-T therapy are described. This review provides the first detailed description of both anticipated and unpredictable hepatic effects of CAR-T cell therapies and is intended to assist in the future characterisation of hepatic effects of CAR-T therapies as programmes move into areas with a different benefit/risk profile, such as autoimmune or other non-oncology indications.

tr.td: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy is a rapidly expanding key therapeutic category, originally pioneered for haematological malignancies, which are now being developed into treatments for solid tumours and non-malignant immune-mediated conditions.

Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has many different adverse effects on the liver and biliary system, and the hepatic effects require a clear understanding to inform the risk:benefit decision of new development programmes.
This review characterises the expected hepatic effects in clinical trial patients receiving CAR-T treatments and provides a framework for the investigation of unexpected liver toxicity.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy is a rapidly expanding important therapeutic category being explored in malignant and non-malignant conditions. Initially developed as cancer immunotherapy, CAR-T therapies use cell engineering techniques to create chimeric antigen receptors on an individual patient’s T cells, with these receptors being able to recognise a protein or antigen expressed on the surface of the target tissue (often a tumour, or immune cells in the case of autoimmune diseases) [1–3]. Chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapies have been most successfully used in haematological malignancies, where six licensed therapies have, so far, shown efficacy in patients refractory to other treatment options, often with long-term disease remission or cure as reviewed previously [4–6].

Despite the ongoing promise of efficacy, CAR-T therapies face several well-characterised and relatively unique challenges, including severe life-threatening toxicities such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS), Immune Effector Cell-Associated Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis-Like Syndrome (IEC-HLH, also known as EIC-HLH or HLH), immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) and prolonged cytopenias [6, 7]. In addition, liver-related adverse events (AEs) and liver test abnormalities have been commonly reported after CAR-T treatment (the term ‘hepatic effects’ is used in this manuscript to describe the composite of liver test changes and adverse hepatic events) [8–25]. These reports are generally from clinical trials, rather than case reports with thorough causality assessment. Interpretation from data within a clinical trial publication is more challenging due to lack of detail to exclude competing aetiologies. Possible mechanisms for these hepatic effects include specific and unusual multi-system inflammatory response toxicities, associated cardiac dysfunction, bacterial or viral infection or reactivation leading to hepatitis including hepatitis B reactivation (HBVr), or other liver-related pathologies [23, 26–32]. However, the hepatic effects of CAR-T treatments are often poorly characterised, with limited review of the underlying potential aetiologies. Despite the frequency of such hepatic effects, the benefit-risk profile for CAR-T treatment for haematological malignancies in heavily pre-treated and refractory patients remains positive.

Chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapies are rapidly expanding into other indications, including solid tumour malignancies, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases and fibrosis [33–38]. The use of CAR-T therapies to treat autoimmune conditions could provide a better understanding of the hepatic effects. Patients with autoimmune diseases may have a normal or overactive immune system and are less likely to have the profound immunosuppression of a highly pre-treated oncology patient. Other important aspects where there may be notable differences include the generally lower doses of CAR-T effector cells used, administering CAR-T in the absence of the pro-inflammatory tumour microenvironment, and more time to medically optimise a patient to receive such therapies. A rigorous liver status assessment at baseline, and reduced confounding of alternative causes of liver test changes, often observed in the oncology population, should allow improved characterisation and identification of liver injury after CAR-T therapies in non-malignant conditions.

Facilitating a thorough benefit-risk assessment in these expanded patient populations requires specific focus on the common organ toxicities, including characterising the frequency and severity of hepatic effects. This literature review and expert consensus summarises the current literature to describe the hepatic toxicity associated with AEs such as CRS and IEC-HLH along with other diagnoses that can impact the liver, including drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and hepatitis B reactivation (HBVr). This review also proposes a clear structure for the investigation of hepatic effects in patients after CAR-T therapy, to enhance data collection in clinical trials. Improved understanding of liver safety and risk mitigation in this fast-expanding development area, by describing the characteristic features such as time in relation to CAR-T administration and pattern of liver injury for the various hepatic effects, will help clinical development programmes assess liver safety signals.

sec.title: Methodology
sec.p: This review was developed by the IQ Consortium (International Consortium for Innovation and Quality in Pharmaceutical Development) DILI Initiative (IQ-DILI): a collaboration across 17 pharmaceutical companies, working with DILI experts from academia and regulatory agencies. The IQ Consortium is a science‐focused, not‐for‐profit organisation addressing scientific and technical aspects of drug development. The IQ-DILI follows clear principles of extensive literature review and carefully structured discussions at IQ-DILI conferences to critically appraise the evidence, and support this with experience and debate, to create consensus around a topic. Previous IQ-DILI consensus reviews following the same principles have already been published, supporting DILI detection and management in many aspects of liver disease and drug development, including non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), viral hepatitis, oncology, immune-mediated liver injury from checkpoint inhibitors and chronic cholestatic liver disease clinical trials, and in patients with cirrhosis [39–43]. The analyses and consensus recommendations provided herein are based on the opinions of the authors following literature review and discussion, and do not imply a regulatory guidance or mandate. The quality of the literature evidence, and the contribution from either scientific evidence or opinion for consensus is not formally rated.

sec.title: Literature Search
sec.p: Relevant publications were identified through searching MEDLINE and EMBASE databases, using search terms for CAR-T, CAR-T brand names, HBV-related terms, and liver-related clinical symptoms and laboratory testing terms (Literature search strategy described in detail in the Supplemental information). Articles from January 2000 until May 2nd, 2024, were included, returning 577 articles. All articles were reviewed for hepatic effects, or for relevant case studies. Of the 577 articles reviewed, 189 publications were included (as described in Supplemental Information Fig. 1)

sec.title: Incidence of Hepatic Effects After CAR-T Therapy
sec.p: Hepatic effects after CAR-T therapy are reported very commonly. Furthermore, liver test changes that are regarded as part of an alternative diagnosis such as CRS are likely under-reported. The most commonly reported liver-related AEs reflect laboratory test elevations considered clinically relevant (such as ‘elevated transaminases’, ‘alanine aminotransferase increase’, ‘AST abnormal’). Review of AE descriptions synonymous with alanine aminotransferase/aspartate aminotransferase (ALT/AST) elevations (across 27 clinical studies described as Phase I/II or beyond, or cohort studies, and summarised in Table 1 in the supplemental information) showed that incidence rates of an increase in ALT ranged from 7 to 54% of patients after CAR-T, with AST elevations reported in 14–69% of patients [8–25, 44–51].

Grading systems for liver-related AEs allow for some assessment of severity of event. For CAR-T studies, the grade (severity) of an AE is usually classified according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) criteria from the USA Department of Health and Human Services, used widely across oncology studies and currently on Version 5. For aminotransferase elevations, ALT and AST are graded in severity as Grade 1 (1–3× the upper limit of normal [ULN]), or 1.5–3× baseline if baseline ALT elevated), Grade 2 (3–5× ULN, or 3–5× baseline if elevated), Grade 3 (5–20× ULN, or 5–20× baseline if elevated) and Grade 4 (>20× ULN or >20× baseline if elevated). The frequency of Grade 3 or greater elevations in ALT (5–20× ULN) ranged from 0 to 8%; although 11 of the 19 studies reported no Grade 3 or greater elevations [8–25]. A similar pattern was observed for AST with a range of 0–10%, with 9 studies not reporting Grade 3 or greater elevations. One meta-analysis specifically reviewed incidence rates for ALT/AST elevations across 2004 patients after CAR-T therapy [52]. Any grade ALT increase occurred in 28% (95% CI 18–43%) and any grade AST increase of 29% (95% CI 24–35%) [52]. The incidence of grade ≥ 3 ALT and AST elevations was 2% (95% CI 1–3%) and 6% (95% CI 3–10%), respectively [52].

Alanine aminotransferase/aspartate aminotransferase elevations are very commonly reported after CAR-T therapy, but other liver test changes are rarely reported. Only four of the 19 studies reporting ALT/AST elevations also reported total bilirubin (TBIL) changes, and only one study reporting a grade 3 TBIL elevation (>3× ULN or >3× baseline, if elevated at study entry), without detail of whether this occurred with concurrent ALT/AST elevation. Few reports commented on ALP elevations, although this may be because the literature is predominantly from the oncology setting, where increased ALP is common in advanced malignancy. In the setting of DILI from immunotherapy in patients with cancer, the challenges of using the CTCAE grading, particularly in those with pre-existing abnormal baseline levels, are well described [40, 53]. The CTCAE grading for liver-related AEs is considered to lack granularity and poorly reflect the severity of the liver injury, better reflected by examining functional liver impairment with a composite of aminotransferase elevations, bilirubin and INR values.

These data show that aminotransferase elevations after CAR-T therapy (without regard to underlying cause) are common and are generally mild to moderate and not typically elevated above 5× ULN (the internationally recognized consensus threshold for acute drug-induced liver injury) [54]. The suggested threshold for diagnosis of DILI requiring ALT/AST >5× ULN is based on the fact that lower-level aminotransferase elevations are common in the population from many alternative clinical causes or may be transient without a clear underlying cause [54].

The current method for reporting liver test changes as AEs in clinical trials results in challenges that likely mean hepatic effects are significantly under-reported after CAR-T therapy. The liver-related AEs reported generally show a wide range of terms that inadequately describe the exact nature of the abnormality. For example, terms such ‘hepatic function disorder’ have been reported in clinical trials. This provides insufficient information whether this relates to aminotransferase elevations with clinical liver dysfunction (represented by TBIL and prothrombin time/international normalised ratio [PT-INR] changes) or whether this term is simply describing aminotransferase elevations. Adverse event reporting may also result in a single report of an event which combines multiple other symptoms and signs; for example, a patient after CAR-T therapy with ALT elevation, AST elevation, hypotension, cardiac dysfunction and fever, may have a single event term of CRS reported, and the hepatic effects are not specifically reported. The potential for under-reporting of liver laboratory test changes is illustrated by the ZUMA-5 pivotal trial of 148 patients with a median follow up of 18 months. Results showed the incidence of increased ALT reported as an AE as 8%, while the actual frequency of ALT elevation as a laboratory abnormality was 58% [55]. This suggests that those involved in the conduct of clinical trials for CAR-T therapies should aim for improved uniformity and precision when using MedDRA® PT terms to describe AEs or laboratory abnormalities. This could involve detailing the relevant constellation of symptoms as components of one overarching diagnosis such as CRS.

Review of the literature confirms that changes in ALT/AST levels, including Grade 3 changes, are commonly observed following CAR-T therapy. However, these changes are likely under-reported and insufficient for accurately characterizing the clinical relevance of liver test alterations and the underlying injury. Key important missing information includes assessment of severity of aminotransferase changes, thorough review of TBIL and INR, and sufficient work-up and data for causality assessment of the liver test changes. Additional useful information could include histological data to understand the liver pathology, and possible use of additional liver injury biomarkers such as CK-18 and GLDH [56, 57], still in development but may help elucidate the mechanism of injury. Given that the most likely causes of hepatic effects after CAR-T therapy relate to cytokine release syndrome (CRS), Immune Effector Cell-Associated Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis-Like Syndrome (IEC-HS, IEC-HLH, HLH), drug-induced liver injury and HBVr, we proceeded to further characterize timing and pattern of these specific hepatic effects.

sec.title: Hepatic Effects Occurring with Cytokine Release Syndrome
sec.p: Cytokine release syndrome is a well-known early toxicity after CAR-T therapy, a systemic inflammatory response to the release of cytokines following CAR-T [26]. This is a very common syndrome observed after CAR-T treatment, with an incidence estimated between 54 and 91% of all patients [58, 59]. In the oncology setting, frequency is increased with higher tumour burden, increased disease distribution, or higher proliferative activity of the disease [58, 59]. It ranges from a mild, influenza-like illness with fever, myalgia, fatigue and headache, to a significant or life-threatening systemic inflammatory response. Severe CRS is characterised by respiratory and cardiovascular compromise, often with other types of multi-organ dysfunction including hepatic dysfunction. Such cases may be fatal from cardiac arrest, respiratory or other multi-organ failure [26, 27]. Early recognition and treatment of CRS appears important for outcome, and management involves supportive care and immunosuppressants such as steroids and tocilizumab (an interleukin [IL]-6 receptor antagonist) [26, 27]. Cytokine-release syndrome after CAR-T therapy has a median onset of 2–7 days, although it ranges from 1–14 days, and is typically resolved within 2–3 weeks after infusion [26, 27, 60, 61].

Hepatic dysfunction is the most common organ dysfunction observed in patients with Grade 3 (G3) or Grade 4 (G4) CRS, present in 64% of patients, and more common than cardiac dysfunction, present in 36% [62]. The term ‘hepatic dysfunction’ is used frequently in the literature but it is not clearly defined whether this relates to liver test changes or clinically relevant hepatic functional impairment. The term ‘liver toxicity’ is also used, with one study reporting ‘liver toxicity’ in 31% of 111 patients requiring ICU care for CRS [63]. The varying terms used to describe these medical concepts are not clearly enough defined to compare incidence rates across different studies. Significant TBIL elevations have been reported in a small proportion of patients with CRS. One pooled analysis of 137 patients from two phase 2 studies reported 108 cases of CRS, and 12 cases (11%) with G3 (>3× ULN) or greater TBIL elevations, of which 11 of the 12 patients (92%) had CRS [64]. However, the proportion of those with TBIL elevations who also had ALT/AST elevations is not reported. Many of the other studies reviewed in Supplemental Table 1 and presenting ALT/AST abnormalities do not refer to TBIL elevations, which seem unusual with the liver test changes observed as part of CRS [8–25, 44–51].

The liver test elevations generally occur at the time of, or closely following, the appearance of CRS. Median time to peak liver test changes after CAR-T ranges from 1 to 5 days after onset or established CRS [62, 65, 66]. In some cases, however, liver test changes may peak up to 2 weeks after CRS onset [65]. A review of case reports specifically describing the time course and magnitude of ALT/AST changes observe ALT ranging from <100 to 536 U/L, and AST from 170 to 1529 U/L, with peak values observed 1–6 days after the onset of G2 or greater CRS [60–63, 65, 67]. The duration of liver test abnormalities was around 15 days (range 8–20 days) [62]. Resolution of liver test changes generally occurred within one month of CAR-T infusion [62] and usually within 7 days of CRS resolving [65].

The magnitude of ALT/AST elevations appears proportionate to the grade of CRS; higher grade ALT/AST elevations (Grade 3 or 4) are convincingly associated with the presence of more severe CRS [64, 68–70]. One study of 30 patients receiving CD-19 CAR-T showed peak ALT median values of 33 (range 8–292) U/L in grade 1–3 CRS, compared with 111 (range 25–801) U/L with Grade 4 or 5 CRS [66]. The AST values were similar to ALT values in Grade 1–3 CRS but increased above ALT values for G4 or 5 CRS, with a peak median AST of 522U/L (range 9–3725) [66]. Similar findings are reported in other studies, with median ALT values of 95 U/L (range 26–748) in Grade ≥3 CRS compared with 198 U/L (50–1238) in G4 or G5 CRS, and median AST values of 103U/L (range 19–1424) in Grade <3 CRS compared with G4 or G5 CRS (median 389 U/L, range 98–1427) [70]. The median values, and the ranges observed, show consistently that a greater magnitude of ALT/AST change is associated with higher grade CRS.

These findings suggest that the magnitude of AST change may be greater than the ALT change in severe CRS, and with a delay between peak CRS (which would be the period of maximal respiratory and circulatory compromise) and the changes in liver tests. These two factors raise the hypothesis that the ALT/AST changes in CRS relate to liver/tissue hypoperfusion, which could have many underlying mechanisms. These include reduced cardiovascular output, peripheral vasodilation, respiratory impairment and reduced oxygenation, or a combination, which can affect the liver. Support for this hypothesis is that a significantly higher AST than ALT, and high values for both, is usually observed in the context of ischaemic hepatic injury, where hypoperfusion of the liver tissue leads to liver cell necrosis, which becomes apparent in very high AST and ALT levels within a few days of injury. Such cases are often accompanied by an extremely elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) representing tissue damage from hypoperfusion, but with notably little bilirubin rise [71]. The CRS biochemical pattern appears to be similar to that of ischaemic or hypoxic liver injury, although such cases of CRS with liver injury in the literature lack parameters important in this interpretation, such as LDH levels and detailed cardiac status including periods of documented hypotension or significantly reduced oxygenation. An alternative explanation for the AST >ALT ratio is cardiac failure, where AST:ALT >1 may be associated with more severe cardiac failure, reflecting AST release from damaged cardiac muscle [72], or global tissue injury releasing AST [69]. However, case reports describing ALT and AST values in detail generally do not provide additional information for interpretation, such as B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) elevation or clinical cardiac manifestations [69, 73, 74]. Further information on the cardiac AEs after CAR-T therapy is provided in Sect. 7.3.

In addition to CRS, another syndrome complicating CAR-T therapy is immune effector cell-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (IEC-HLH), discussed in detail in Sect. 5. Grade 3–4 elevation of ALT/AST is common in both syndromes but increases in TBIL occur much more often in IEC-HLH. Both syndromes need to be considered in patients after CAR-T therapy presenting with marked transaminase elevations. Features of CRS, and comparison to HLH, are shown in Table 1. sec.title: Hepatic Effects Occurring in Immune Effector Cell-Associated Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (IEC-HLH)
sec.p: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), is a primary (familial) or secondary disorder of severe hyperinflammatory syndrome, with activation of T cells and macrophages, inducing a cascade of cytokine-mediated toxicities [28, 59]. Secondary HLH after CAR-T therapy, due to its specific characteristics, is termed immune effector cell-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome (abbreviated to IEC-HLH, or EIC-HS, or HLH), following an American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) working group review of this specific entity [28]. The overall incidence of IEC-HLH is relatively rare after CAR-T treatment compared to CRS, with an incidence of approximately 3.5% [75]. A reliable feature of IEC-HLH is a significant elevation of ferritin. Thus, while diagnostic criteria for IEC-HLH vary, the CAR T cell-therapy-associated Toxicity (CARTOX) working group suggesting elevated ferritin of >10,000 ng/mL, along with at least two organ toxicities, including the presence of haemophagocytosis in bone marrow or organs, or at least Grade 3 aminotransferase (AT) elevation, renal insufficiency, or pulmonary oedema [75]. Others propose alternative thresholds for ferritin, or ferritins rapidly rising regardless of absolute value, but still in combination with significant (>5× ULN) AT elevations [28]. Although the ferritin thresholds used for diagnosis vary, many cases have ferritin levels above 50,000 ng/L [76]. A normal serum ferritin level usually reliably excludes HLH [77] and should prompt considerations of alternative aetiologies [28]. There is very limited literature on the time to onset of peak ALT/AST elevations compared with peak ferritin, but case reports suggest significant variability, with 7 cases showing peak ALT/AST from a few days before peak ferritin, up to around 15 days after peak ferritin [78–81].

A clear distinction between CRS and IEC-HLH is still debated, which is logical given that both have common mechanisms of systemic inflammation, and that clinical presentations may overlap [69]. One distinguishing feature may be when IEC-HLH presents as a second inflammatory wave after initial improvement in CRS symptoms and signs [69, 73] (see Fig. 1c). Most cases of HLH have therefore been observed with antecedent CRS, with higher grade CRS particularly associated with the development of IEC-HLH [73, 82]. The median time to onset for IEC-HLH is 4–14 days after CRS [28, 69, 83, 84], although it can present up to 2 months after resolution of CRS [28, 84, 85] or, rarely, even up to 1 year after CAR-T [86]. The median duration of IEC-HLH is around 5 days [80].

Grade 3 or higher (>5× ULN) aminotransferase elevation is one of the most common manifestations of IEC-HLH [28, 87, 88] and form part of the proposed diagnostic criteria for HLH [75, 88]. While there may also be evidence of significant hepatic dysfunction, IEC-HLH rarely leads to acute liver failure in adults [89]. Published cohorts of IEC-HLH patients generally show that all patients with HLH have significant aminotransferase elevations [61, 80, 84, 90], often in higher magnitude than in CRS alone [91]. Peak values for ALT and AST presented in a case series of 21 patients with IEC-HLH showed median (range) ALT values of 259 U/L (57–1670 U/L) and AST 568 U/L (64–1464 U/L) [61].

The persistence of liver test elevations when CRS is resolving may suggest developing IEC-HLH. A comparison of patients with CRS alone, compared with CRS then IEC-HLH, shows that mean aminotransferase levels are higher with CRS and subsequent IEC-HLH [92]. Patients eventually developing IEC-HLH have significant differences in ALT and AST levels evident from Day 3 after onset of CRS, and significant differences in TBIL are evident from Day 5 after onset of CRS [61], compared with those who do not go on to experience IEC-HLH. For cases with significant aminotransferase elevations from CRS, a frequent finding is AST exceeding ALT, discussed in Sect. 4, and hypothesised to relate to cardiorespiratory instability and relative liver hypoxia. However, in IEC-HLH, there is no consistent pattern with regard to the release of ALT compared to AST, indicating an alternative mechanism of liver injury compared with CRS [61, 78–81].

Total bilirubin elevations are also more common in IEC-HLH compared with CRS, with elevations above ULN in >50% of patients, with around 33% of patients with TBIL >2× ULN, and TBIL may exceed >5× ULN [61, 93]. This may be multifactorial, relating to liver injury from inflammation/cytokine release, increased haemolysis and phagocytosis of red blood cells. However, direct hyperbilirubinaemia may also be present, suggesting that haemolysis alone may not fully account for such changes [28].

Given the close association between IEC-HLH and ALT/AST and TBIL elevations, hepatic effects are anticipated with IEC-HLH; the ASTCT working group suggested that the absence of aminotransferase or TBIL elevations should prompt consideration of alternate diagnoses and not IEC-HLH. However, the hepatic effects do not tend to dominate the clinical picture or appear in relative isolation with few other features. Therefore, ASTCT recommends that a predominance and/or persistence of a liver injury pattern, where the liver injury is dominant compared with other features of HLH, should trigger evaluation for underlying causes of hepatic injury other than IEC-HLH [28]. An illustrative representation of liver test change onset, peak and resolution for IEC-HLH following high grade CRS is shown in Fig. 1c.

sec.title: Other Hepatic Effects Reported after CAR-T Treatment
Clinical Trial-Related Hepatic Effects without Apparent CRS or IEC-HLH
sec.p: There are case reports of hepatic effects following CAR-T therapy that are not reported concurrently with CRS or IEC-HLH, but these publications have few clinical details and causality cannot be fully assessed. These reports include treatment-related acute hepatic failure without CRS/IEC-HLH within the first two months after CAR-T therapy [23, 97]; hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome within a few months of CAR-T [98], early immune-related hepatitis [99], Grade 3 or greater aminotransferase elevations without CRS or IEC-HLH [3], liver ‘damage’ requiring additional monitoring [100] and reports of liver-related dose-limiting toxicity in early phase studies [101]. There are also reports of aminotransferase elevations relating to CAR-T treatment occurring up to 2 years after CAR-T [102]. These publications lack sufficient detail for causality assessment. Moreover, they lack a mechanistic understanding of CAR-T–related liver injury as none of the CAR-T directed targets from the cases described above are expressed on healthy (non-malignant) liver tissue. For improved understanding of such cases where there are significant hepatic effects not related to CRS or IEC-HLH, a liver biopsy could provide useful mechanistic information for either detecting a clear alternative cause, or unexpected expression of the CAR-T cell target antigen (see Sect. 6.3).

sec.title: Post-Marketing/Real World Data Review
sec.p: Post-marketing and registry safety data also suggest rare cases of liver toxicity attributed directly to CAR-T therapy. The European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (EBMT) registry of 492 patients showed 6 cases (2%) with severe liver toxicity (defined as Grade 3 or greater) in the first 100 days after CAR-T therapy [60]. Of these cases, half had liver toxicity without other major organ toxicity, and events occurred up to Day 100 after CAR-T [60].

A review of post-marketing safety using the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) [103], identified a new potential safety signal of hepatic failure with the specific CAR-T tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel). Post-marketing reports are coded using the global Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA®), which standardises how events are reported in order to facilitate safety signal detection. MedDRA® is organised into 5 hierarchy levels, and the MedDRA® ‘Higher Level Term (HLT)’ is used to group together the multiple terms that are related to the same medical concept. Sixteen cases of drug-related hepatic failure (cases with terms defined within the ‘Hepatic failure and associated disorders’ higher level MedDRA® term) were reported in patients treated with Tisa-cel, which was disproportionately higher than cases of hepatic failure observed for axicabtagene ciloleucel (Axi-cel), or for other agents used to treat the same therapeutic indication. In addition, 6 cases of terms collected within the higher-level term of ‘jaundice and cholestasis’ were reported, also with an increased frequency compared to comparator or other treatments, although the overlap between these cases and cases in the ‘hepatic failure and associated disorders’ category is not described. Most (13 of the 16) cases of hepatic failure also reported CRS. The authors suggested that hepatic failure and jaundice and cholestasis may represent new safety signals. A similar finding was observed using the WHO Vigibase database, where there was a disproportionate association between CAR-T and hepatic events compared with other drugs in the database; of the 32 reports of the ADR subclass ‘hepatic injury’ (a categorisation not formal to MedDRA® but a grouping which incorporated the terms Cholestasis, Hepatic failure, Hepatic necrosis, Hepatomegaly, Hepatosplenomegaly, Hyperbilirubinaemia, Hypoalbuminaemia), 23 were associated with CRS, 7 with CRS/HLH and 2 without other organ toxicity [104]. These studies used post-marketing disproportionality assessment, a statistical method for detecting an unexpected frequency of an event with a particular drug, compared to an appropriate control, to detect potential safety signals. Although this type of study has limitations, it provides a useful prompt that further evaluation of hepatic events after CAR-T therapy is warranted.

sec.title: DILI After CAR-T Therapy
sec.p: Many hepatic effects are reported as a consequence of CAR-T treatment, although it is difficult to characterise these as DILI without a better understanding of mechanism and the clinical consequences of the frequently reported aminotransferase and bilirubin elevations following CAR-T. The three main types of DILI are direct, idiosyncratic and indirect, which vary widely by latency, incidence, and pathogenesis [105]. Direct DILI is generally dose-related with a rapid onset that occurs in a high proportion of exposed individuals and can usually be predicted to some extent by preclinical toxicology. In the setting of CAR-T and liver injury, direct injury could occur when these cells engage their target antigen via specific recognition and exert cytotoxic effects through direct contact [106]. Dose limiting liver toxicity leading to product termination occurred in patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma who received anti-carboxy-anhydrase-IX (CAIX) CAR-T cells, dosed daily for 5 days [107]. Liver biopsy revealed discrete cholangitis with T-cell infiltration around the bile ducts [107, 108]. Mechanistically, this was confirmed as direct DILI, with the on-target but off-tumour activity of CAR-T against CAIX expression, expressed by renal cell tumours but also on bile duct epithelial cells [107, 108]. Flow cytometry confirmed the presence specifically of CAR-T cells within the liver biopsy specimen [107, 108]. Direct DILI is rare, particularly with the pre-clinical models available to assess potential hepatotoxicity and target expression in liver tissue before proceeding to human studies (see Sect. 9).

Indirect DILI, exemplified by check-point inhibitors, occurs when major negative immune regulators are blocked, making the liver susceptible to immune-mediated AEs. This type of DILI has not yet been reported following CAR-T therapy. Identifying the more ‘usual’ idiosyncratic DILI during CAR-T therapy is very difficult, given the high frequency of hepatotoxicity with CRS, the large variety of other known causes of hepatotoxicity that occur during such therapy, and the lack of specific markers for DILI. The disorders that confound the diagnosis of DILI include not only CRS and IEC-HLH, but also the other causes discussed in Sect. 7. Thus, diagnosing idiosyncratic DILI following CAR-T therapy to explain elevations of transaminase and/or bilirubin without other explanation is a very difficult challenge.

sec.title: Characteristics of Alternative Causes of Hepatic Effects after CAR-T Therapy
sec.p:
Standard practice in clinical trials is for close monitoring of liver tests as the liver safety profile (clinical signature) of an agent is explored. Guidance around detection and assessment of DILI in clinical trials describes the importance of comprehensive investigations to exclude alternative causes, as DILI is often a diagnosis of exclusion [109, 110]. However, clinical trial participants in CAR-T therapies have an additional set of relatively unique causes of liver test changes to be considered in addition to those encountered more frequently across clinical trials. These include infections, viral reactivations including HBV, Chronic Hepatitis E infection (HEV) infection, cytomegalovirus infection (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus infection (EBV), Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), and the multiple concomitant medications used to manage infection, neurological toxicity, CRS and other conditions [111–119]. Alternative causes which may affect more than 5% of CAR-T recipients are reviewed below, with their approximate frequency and time to onset illustrated in Fig. 2 [23, 26, 27, 29–31, 59–62, 65, 66, 73, 80, 83–86, 91, 114, 116–118, 120–130]. sec.title: Infection After CAR-T Therapy
sec.p: The incidence of infections is high after CAR-T therapy, likely from multifactorial immunosuppression including past immunosuppressive or chemotherapy treatments, lymphodepletion prior to CAR-T, cytokine-related cytopenias, and hypogammaglobulinaemia after CAR-T. Estimated incidence of infections within the first 30 days ranges from 23 to 36% [120–122]. Around one-third of these early infections are severe, requiring intravenous antibiotics or hospitalization [122]. Bacterial infections tend to dominate early after CAR-T for the first 30 days [29, 123], and an increased risk persists to 1 year or beyond [27]. The timing of bacterial infection overlaps with neutropenia and CRS but typically follows the onset of CRS [124]. Severe bacterial infections are frequently associated with aminotransferase, ALP, and bilirubin elevations, particularly those leading to sepsis [131–133]. The most frequent pattern is of cholestatic injury, sometimes called ‘cholestasis of sepsis’, with hyperbilirubinaemia often reported in the range of 2–10 mg/dL [132], and accompanying ALP elevations, although modest aminotransferase elevations [133]. Cholestasis of sepsis generally resolves with successful treatment of the underlying infection.

Viral infection may be newly acquired or a re-activation. Examples of newly acquired infections include common respiratory viruses like influenza and respiratory syncytial virus, which can be rare causes of liver injury [134–136]. Some viruses acquired through past infection can establish latency in the host genome and therefore have the potential to reactivate with periods of immunosuppression. These viral infections include HBV, EBV, CMV, VZV and HSV, all of which may lead to clinical hepatitis. Patients should be tested for these viruses prior to CAR-T to understand baseline status. Viral infections/reactivations are unusual in the immediate post-CAR-T period and tend to dominate beyond 28 days after CAR-T therapy [121], and throughout the rest of the first year after CAR-T [124]. In one study, one quarter of CAR-T-treated patients experienced viral infections/reactivation, most frequently CMV, followed by EBV and Herpes Zoster, and HBV reactivation (see Sect. 7.4) [112]. The time to onset for CMV, EBV and herpes zoster ranged from 30 to around 500 days post-CAR-T infusion. For CMV infection specifically, all reactivations occurred within the first 6 months; however, for EBV, 3 of the 4 cases occurred after 6 months [112]. Hepatitis C and E infections, both acute and chronic, should also be considered [119]. Fungal infections are rarer than bacterial or viral infections [29, 137], which may relate to the widespread use of antifungal prophylaxis.

In addition to bacterial and viral infections causing primary or secondary hepatitis, treatments of such infections may also be a rare cause of liver injury. Anti-infective agents are a major class of drug frequently linked with drug-induced liver injury (DILI), whether used for treatment or prophylaxis. The most frequently used antimicrobials covering CAR-T therapy include fluroquinolone antibiotics, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis Jirovecii prophylaxis, and azole antifungals, all well-known to cause DILI [138]. Antimicrobial treatment, and particularly intravenous agents, have a strong association with DILI [139]. However, due to the challenges in diagnosing DILI caused by infective agents in patients following CAR-T therapy, where multiple concurrent medications are involved, no data are currently available to determine the frequency of such cases.

sec.title: Liver Toxicity Secondary to Other Concomitant Medications for CAR-T Treatment
sec.p: A common toxicity specific to CAR-T treatment requiring potentially liver-toxic concomitant medications is ICANS (Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome). This is a frequent toxicity of CAR-T treatment, with neurological deficits, seizures and coma [140], estimated to occur in 37.5–77% of patients after CAR-T treatment [125]. The mean time to onset is early, approximately 4–6 days, with mean duration around 8 days [59, 125], although it can be bi-phasic with a second peak around 1 month after CAR-T therapy [126]. Treatment of symptoms of ICANS may involve many medications, which can be associated with liver injury (although rare), including levetiracetam, phenobarbital and other antiseizure medications, and acetazolamide to reduce intracranial pressure.

A further consideration for liver-toxic medications includes the preparation for CAR-T treatment of lymphocyte depletion conditioning to prepare for infusion for CAR-T cells. Typically, fludarabine/high dose cyclophosphamide combination is used [141, 142]. Higher-dose cyclophosphamide may be associated with liver injury and acute sinusoidal obstruction syndrome generally appearing within 10–20 days of myeloablation [143]. Fludarabine has been associated with mild, self-limiting liver injury, but no specific time to onset has yet been characterised [144].

sec.title: Cardiac-Related Secondary Liver Injury
sec.p: Cardiac compromise is common after CAR-T treatment, estimated in around 12–28% of patients, and may result in cardiovascular (CV)-related death or decompensated heart failure [30, 31, 127]. Median time to onset is 5–21 days after CAR-T treatment [30, 31, 127], although it can occur up to 5 months after CAR-T infusion [31]. Cardiac toxicity is usually, but not always, associated with CRS [30, 145]. A recent meta-analysis across 23 CAR-T trials showed a prevalence rate of 17% for atrial fibrillation (95% CI 8–29%), 7% for cardiac arrest (95% CI 2–14%), 30% for heart failure (95% CI 16–47%), and 2% for cardiac mortality (95% CI 1–3%) in patients who had received CAR T-cell therapy [146]. Cardiac manifestations most commonly include profound hypotension, but also sinus tachycardia, elevations in serum troponin levels, left-ventricular systolic dysfunction, myocardial infarction, decompensated heart failure, new-onset arrhythmias, and cardiovascular death [147–149]. Hepatic dysfunction can therefore occur from either congestion from increased filling pressures or low cardiac output and resulting impaired perfusion [150]. Acute changes in cardiac function leading to ischaemic liver injury classically present with very high aminotransferase levels acutely, with AST values notably greater than ALT [71, 151]. There may also be LDH elevations (usually of higher magnitude than ALT elevations) and creatine phosphokinase elevations, along with transient elevated creatinine representing the effects of the ischaemia on the kidneys [71, 151, 152]. Conversely, congestive cardiac impairment may present with a more cholestatic or mixed pattern of liver injury. This is considered to relate to impaired biliary drainage secondary to hepatic venous congestion and generally presents with only mild or modest increases in ALT/AST (in the absence of concurrent ischaemia). For liver test changes where cardiac causes are plausible, there may be additional laboratory biomarkers or imaging tests to support a cardiac cause, including elevated b-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), or troponin elevations, ECG changes and reduced ejection fraction on echocardiogram [146, 153].

sec.title: Hepatitis B Reactivation Associated with Immunosuppressant or Immunomodulating Drugs
sec.p: Hepatitis B reactivation (HBVr) associated with immunosuppressant or immunomodulating (IS/IM) drugs is an important cause of morbidity and mortality in patients who have current or prior exposure to HBV [154–157]. Hepatitis B reactivation is a form of indirect hepatotoxicity [105] and can lead to severe liver injury or liver failure, with consequences of liver transplantation or death, but it is often preventable through prophylactic antiviral therapy and close monitoring [154–157]. Liver transplantation is likely not an option for CAR-T cell recipients treated for malignancy but may be an option for patients treated for immune-related diseases.

Several consensus guideline publications on prevention and treatment of HBVr during IS/IM drug therapy classified the risk of HBVr into low (<1%), moderate (1%–10%), and high (>10%) risk categories [155–158]. These risk categories are used to guide medical decisions regarding monitoring and prophylactic treatment to detect and decrease the risk of HBVr during and after IS/IM therapy. In general, individuals’ HBV serologic status has a significant effect on the risk of HBVr. Reactivation is more likely among patients who are HBsAg-positive than those with resolved HBV infection, defined in most guidelines as those who are HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc–positive, and HBV DNA–negative [154–157]. Prophylactic treatment with nucleos(t)ide analogues (NA) has been shown to substantially reduce the risk of HBVr when started prior to the initiation of IS/IM therapy [154, 158].

sec.title: HBV Reactivation Associated with CAR-T in HBsAg-Positive Patients
sec.p: To date, there have been 11 studies or reports in patients with evidence of resolved or current HBV infection who received CAR-T therapy (Supplemental Table 2) [116–118, 128, 129]. The risk of HBVr in CAR-T recipients who are HBsAg-positive and are naïve to treatment for HBV could not be calculated since in all studies, patients who were HBsAg-positive were receiving antiviral prophylaxis.

The decision to initiate HBV prophylaxis in HBsAg-positive patients receiving CAR-T is supported by several reasons: (1) the general immunodeficiency state related to the underlying disease (e.g., leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma); (2) patients who received CAR-T therapy were often treated with multiple agents with IM/IS effect, which increase the risk of HBVr; and (3) often these patients had been treated with medications that have a long-lasting IS/IM effect (e.g., B cell–depleting agents) prior to initiation of CAR-T. Interestingly, a meta-analysis of HBsAg-positive patients receiving CAR-T therapy, showed 11% HBVr despite prophylactic therapy with NAs [157]. Based on these considerations, recent consensus guidelines have classified HBsAg-positive patients undergoing CAR-T therapy as high risk for HBVr (>10%) [154, 156, 157]. As such, recent consensus recommendations by several groups call for initiating anti-viral prophylaxis with NAs prior to CAR-T therapy in HBsAg-positive patients. Such patients should also continue close monitoring of liver tests and HBV DNA every 1–3 months [154, 156, 157].

sec.title: HBV Reactivation Associated with CAR-T in HBsAg-Negative/ANTI-HBc-Positive Patients
sec.p: In a recently published clinical practice guideline from the American Gastroenterology Association (AGA) [157], a pooled sample of 161 patients demonstrated that the risk of HBVr in HBsAg-negative/anti-HBc-positive patients undergoing CAR-T therapy was 21 per 1000 (2.1%), classifying this population group to be at a moderate risk of reactivation. However, some patients included in this risk calculation were on NA prophylaxis. These results were similar to a recent meta-analysis by Papatheodoridis et al [154], which showed a pooled risk of 4% (confidence intervals 1–9%). Based on these data, Papatheodoridis et al [154] recommended monitoring ALT and HBV DNA in HBsAg-negative/anti-HBc-positive patients and deciding on the need for NA according to the results.

In contrast, the more conservative AGA guideline [157] recommended initiating prophylactic therapy prior to the CAR-T therapy in all HBsAg-negative/anti-HBc-positive patients [157]. This is because AGA classified these patients as high risk for HBVr, given the complexity of these patients combined with the expectation that this population will receive multiple concomitant IS/IM medications including B cell–depleting agents such as rituximab, which are classified as high-risk for HBVr [157].

sec.title: HCV Reactivation/Enhanced Replication
sec.p: The potential for reactivation/enhanced replication of HCV infection after CAR-T is not yet well defined, although studies in other immunosuppressive cancer treatment suggest a very small risk of reactivation, and mostly with an unremarkable clinical course [130, 159, 160]. Monitoring for reactivation/enhanced replication has been proposed, but without clear detail [161]. Re-infection with HCV should also be considered.

sec.title: Coagulation Disorders
sec.p: Coagulation disorders affecting liver function, including venous thromboembolism and disseminated intravascular coagulation, have been reported. Venous or arterial thromboembolism or clinically relevant bleeding episodes are common after CAR-T therapy, generally occurring within the first 1–3 months and affecting 6%–11% of patients [162–168]. Rare secondary liver-related effects reported include portal vein thrombosis and liver dysfunction from microthromboembolic disease [167, 168].

sec.title: Recommended Evaluation of Patients with Liver Test Abnormalities After CAR-T Treatment
sec.p:
Many patients after CAR-T treatment will develop hepatic effects secondary to other toxicities; those with hepatic effects characteristic for either CRS or HLH may not need additional investigations if the diagnosis is considered well established. However, patients with CRS or HLH who present without the typical clinical picture or where hepatic effects are dissociated from CRS or IEC-HLH require a comprehensive evaluation for alternative causes of liver injury. Detailed evaluation allows for a robust causality assessment of the role of the CAR-T therapy in causing the hepatic effects. sec.title: Predicting CAR-T Liver Toxicity: Nonclinical Risk Assessment for Potential Hepatotoxicity
sec.p: There is a range of available preclinical models and tools to assess engineered T-cell-associated toxicities that has been reviewed extensively by Donnardieu et al. [175]. However, challenges remain as these models have not been developed to specifically assess CAR-T-induced hepatotoxicity. There are in vivo models where hepatotoxicity of CAR-T cells has been assessed in addition to efficacy endpoints [176–180], although the translatability of these findings to humans is not clear. In addition, while novel in vivo toxicology models have been recently generated to address on target/off-tumour-driven toxicities, the suitability and feasibility of these models need to be confirmed [106, 181].

In addition to in vivo models, there have been some efforts to develop sensitive methods such as RNAscope in situ hybridization (ISH) technologies that enable detection of low level of Ag expression on normal human tissues at the preclinical stage, especially when using low antigen-density-tuned CAR-Ts. This technology has been suggested for utilisation in preclinical assessment of CAR-T safety/toxicity [182] and could be an addition to the preclinical screening models for future studies.

Taken together, the available pre-clinical strategies for assessing CAR-T–induced hepatotoxicity risks are imperfect. While recent in vivo models have enhanced the predictiveness of these models, these approaches are rarely used clinically and still might not accurately reflect the complex expression patterns of tumour-associated antigens or immune cell antigens on non-malignant, non-target human tissues. An important area of research is to refine animal models and/or organ-on-a-chip technologies to predict these toxicities more accurately. Therefore, when commencing first-in-human drug development, it is important to understand that the pre-clinical models may have limitations regarding prediction of hepatotoxicity.

sec.title: Expanding Understanding of Hepatic Effects in an Era of New, Non-oncology Indications
sec.p: The use of CAR-T therapies to treat autoimmune conditions as well as cancer could provide a better understanding of the hepatic effects. Patients with autoimmune diseases may have a normal or overactive immune system and are less likely to have the profound immunosuppression of a highly pre-treated oncology patient. From one perspective, these patients with more intact immune systems may show increased immune-mediated events, including hepatic events. However, CAR-T programmes in non-oncology indications generally use a lower number of CAR-T cells as the overall treatment aim is immune system regulation rather than complete elimination of a cancer. Such lower doses, and the absence of the tumour microenvironment, which may release pro-inflammatory cytokines, may significantly decrease the systemic inflammation accompanying CAR-T treatment, and better allow for the detection and characterisation of hepatic effects after CAR-T. Although most CAR-T therapies for non-malignant diseases are still in pre-clinical or early-phase trials in progress, two published phase 1 trials (one in lupus nephritis and one in HIV) report only mild CRS, and do not report hepatic effects [183, 184]. However, CAR-T cells transferred for autoimmunity indications appear to have a significantly shorter persistence than those used in the oncology setting. The reasons for this are still not clear, but shorter persistence and lower dose may reduce the frequency and severity of immune-related adverse effects [185]. European EBMT recommendations for CAR-T in autoimmunity include liver-related eligibility criteria and exclusion of those with active liver disease [186]. Furthermore, they recommend that it is mandatory to clearly identify the underlying causes of any abnormal liver chemistry at baseline [186]. This rigorous liver status assessment at baseline, and the reduction of confounding alternative causes of liver test changes, often observed in the oncology population, should allow better characterisation and identification of liver injury after CAR-T therapies in non-malignant conditions. Efforts to characterise clinical variables that influence the risk of developing liver injury should also be explored.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapies have a wide range of hepatic effects through specific toxicities or adverse effects from the treatment used to address toxicities, the potential for drug-induced liver injury as well as viral hepatitis/reactivation. Many of these toxicities are specific to CAR-T therapies and are not frequently observed in clinical trials of other therapies. Data describing characteristic hepatic effects in CRS and IEC-HLH are emerging, and more data are required. Patients with characteristic hepatic effects in the context of CRS or IEC-HLH should be closely monitored. Patients with atypical hepatic effects, or clinical liver injury, which is often complex in this patient population, should have a comprehensive assessment of alternative causes performed. By proposing a structured approach to routine, first-line and second-line liver-related investigations, this review aims to improve the future characterisation of hepatic effects of CAR-T therapies as programmes move into areas with a different benefit/risk profile, such as autoimmune or other non-oncology indications.
